findings.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — [confidence 100, P2] Concurrent checks of the same email lose recorded matches because `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` performs an unlocked read-modify-write, so two requests reading count N both persist N+1 and the later write can also move `last_match_at` backwards; update the count atomically and preserve timestamp ordering.

lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — [confidence 75, P2] Calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` from validation makes match statistics depend on the caller's validation and transaction structure: `User.create_for_email` calls `user.save!` at app/models/user.rb:103, so rejection rolls back the nested `record.save` at app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 and leaves the attempted match unrecorded, while a successful `:do_nothing` signup validates at both app/controllers/users_controller.rb:168 and :172 and records two matches for one attempt; separate the policy predicate from attempt accounting at a transaction boundary that survives rejection.

app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:69 — [confidence 100, P3, advisory] After a signup rejection followed by an administrator removing the email block or changing the provider restriction, `if (this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email))` still disables submission through `emailValidation.failed` with no invalidation path, preventing the now-eligible applicant from retrying until the page reloads; delete the persistent cache at line 17, the rejection branch at lines 69–74, its dependency at line 96, and cache insertion at lines 274–276 while retaining the server's error flash, and although the strongest rebuttal is that caching avoids futile submissions, it fails because the cached decision outlives the mutable server policy that produced it.

app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:274 — P1, confidence 75: after a signup fails only because its username became unavailable, `if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values)` treats the serialized `email: []` as an error and `createAccountController.get('rejectedEmails').pushObject(result.values.email);` permanently disables resubmission with the valid email even after the username is corrected, because the new validator's `record.errors[attribute].blank?` inserts that empty array into the legacy ActiveModel errors hash and `user.errors.to_hash` preserves it ([Rails source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rails/rails/v3.2.13/activemodel/lib/active_model/errors.rb)); the strongest rebuttal that the server supplies only actual errors fails for this empty-array entry, and a direct execution of the changed controller with that response reproduces `emailValidation.failed: true`.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — P2, confidence 100: two simultaneous matches that both read count N execute `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save`, write N+1 twice, and silently lose one match from the administrator's statistics while both calls return their ordinary block decision, with an older `record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now` also able to overwrite a newer timestamp when saves complete out of order; the strongest rebuttal that saving and the unique email index serialize updates fails because neither locks the initial read nor makes the increment atomic.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — Confidence 75, P2: `record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` compares unnormalized addresses in a string column, so a blocked mailbox registered as `block@spamfromhome.org` can evade the new signup block by submitting `block@SPAMFROMHOME.ORG`, whose domain identifies the same mailbox but does not match the stored string; the strongest rebuttal is upstream email normalization, but `User.new_from_params` assigns `user.email = params[:email]` directly and this model also preserves mixed-case blocklist entries, so the control must canonicalize both stored and submitted addresses to protect site moderators from repeat registrations.

spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:7 — Advisory (confidence 100, P2): `subject(:validate) { validator.validate_each(record,:email,record.email) }` bypasses the newly changed User validation registration in every validator example, so removing `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` leaves all supplied blocking tests unchanged while real blocked-email registrations succeed; the strongest rebuttal is that separate validator and BlockedEmail unit tests cover each component, but neither invokes User validation, so add a real blocked-record example through User validation and an unchanged-email lifecycle example.

spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb:22 — Advisory (confidence 100, P2): `it "returns false if a record with the email doesn't exist" do` executes against an empty blocked-email table, making these examples equally satisfied by `BlockedEmail.first` in place of the email-filtered lookup and leaving rejection of unrelated users undetected once any block entry exists; the strongest rebuttal is that matching-record examples also exercise lookup, but their sole row always matches the requested email, so add a nonmatching persisted row and assert both acceptance and unchanged statistics.

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real transactional issue. Looking at the diff: BlockedEmail.should_block? (lines 11-17 in blocked_email.rb) calls record.save to update match_count and last_match_at. This is called from EmailValidator.validate_each (line 13 in email_validator.rb) during validation. If the user creation fails and rolls back, the BlockedEmail statistics update would also be rolled back since it's within the same transaction. Additionally, if validation runs multiple times (as the finding suggests with validate at lines 168 and 172), statistics could be recorded multiple times. The core issue - mixing side effects (statistics recording) with validation logic that may be rolled back or called multiple times - is a legitimate bug in the diff's design.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:69 — [confidence 100, P3, advisory] After a signup rejection followed by an administrator removing the email block or changing the provider restriction, `if (this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email))` still disables submission through `emailValidation.failed` with no invalidation path, preventing the now-eligible applicant from retrying until the page reloads; delete the persistent cache at line 17, the rejection branch at lines 69–74, its dependency at line 96, and cache insertion at lines 274–276 while retaining the server's error flash, and although the strongest rebuttal is that caching avoids futile submissions, it fails because the cached decision outlives the mutable server policy that produced it.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real issue in the diff. The code at line 17 initializes `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])`, and lines 69-74 check if an email is in this array to block submission. Lines 274-276 add rejected emails to this array when the server returns an error. The problem is that this client-side cache persists for the session, so if an admin removes an email block or changes whitelist/blacklist settings, the user cannot retry with the same email until they reload the page. The cache has no invalidation mechanism and outlives the server-side policy that created it. This is a legitimate UX bug where valid emails could be incorrectly blocked on the client side.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:274 — P1, confidence 75: after a signup fails only because its username became unavailable, `if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values)` treats the serialized `email: []` as an error and `createAccountController.get('rejectedEmails').pushObject(result.values.email);` permanently disables resubmission with the valid email even after the username is corrected, because the new validator's `record.errors[attribute].blank?` inserts that empty array into the legacy ActiveModel errors hash and `user.errors.to_hash` preserves it ([Rails source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rails/rails/v3.2.13/activemodel/lib/active_model/errors.rb)); the strongest rebuttal that the server supplies only actual errors fails for this empty-array entry, and a direct execution of the changed controller with that response reproduces `emailValidation.failed: true`.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that `record.errors[attribute].blank?` in the EmailValidator inserts an empty array into the errors hash, but this is incorrect. The `.blank?` method only reads from the errors hash, it doesn't write to it. Looking at the diff, `record.errors.add(attribute, ...)` is only called when validation fails (whitelist/blacklist violations or blocked email). The `user.errors.to_hash` in the controller would only contain actual error messages that were added via `errors.add()`. There's no mechanism shown in this diff where an empty array would be inserted for the email field. The finding misunderstands how ActiveModel errors work - checking `.blank?` doesn't create an entry.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:7 — Advisory (confidence 100, P2): `subject(:validate) { validator.validate_each(record,:email,record.email) }` bypasses the newly changed User validation registration in every validator example, so removing `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` leaves all supplied blocking tests unchanged while real blocked-email registrations succeed; the strongest rebuttal is that separate validator and BlockedEmail unit tests cover each component, but neither invokes User validation, so add a real blocked-record example through User validation and an unchanged-email lifecycle example.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a testing gap: the new EmailValidator spec tests the validator in isolation by calling validate_each directly, and the BlockedEmail spec tests the model independently. Neither test actually exercises the full User validation path that includes `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`. If someone removed that line from User.rb, the existing tests would still pass because they don't go through User validation. The finding suggests adding integration-level tests that validate through the User model to ensure the validator is properly wired up. This is a legitimate test coverage concern for newly added validation logic, not a bug but an important gap in test coverage.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a test coverage gap in the new spec file. Looking at the diff, the test 'returns false if a record with the email doesn't exist' runs against an empty table, and the 'when a BlockedEmail record matches' examples only create a single record that matches the queried email. The finding's concern is valid: if `should_block?` were implemented as `BlockedEmail.first` instead of `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, these tests would still pass. Adding a non-matching persisted row would strengthen the test. This is a legitimate test coverage concern for newly added code, not a bug in production code.
